Action Plan:
1. Provide acute symptom relief: patient to take ibuprofen (dose/route/frequency not documented) together with an over-the-counter anti-sickness preparation (name/dose/route/frequency not documented) and a sugary, carbonated drink (e.g., cola) immediately.  
2. Arrange same-day face-to-face GP appointment for full neurological examination; patient advised she may cancel if headache settles before the slot.  
3. Safety-net: instruct patient to attend Emergency Department urgently if headache worsens, new neurological deficits develop, vomiting persists, or pain lasts >72 hours.  
4. Reassure and address health anxiety; explained likely migraine etiology and variability of age of onset.  
5. Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
• Reason for visit: sudden left-sided headache with visual disturbance.  
• HPI:  
  – Onset: abrupt this morning (~4 h ago).  
  – Location: left side of head; sometimes felt “behind the eye.”  
  – Intensity: 6/10 (kidney-stone pain =10/10 reference).  
  – Character: throbbing, worsens with movement; patient prefers lying still.  
  – Associated symptoms: blurred vision with zig-zag lines, dizziness, photophobia (unable to tolerate screens), nausea, 2 episodes of vomiting.  
  – Medications tried: paracetamol taken ~3 h prior, no relief.  
• Past medical history: kidney stones. No previous migraines.  
• Family history: mother—migraines and hypothyroidism.  
• Medications: none regularly. Paracetamol today (dose/route/frequency not documented).  
• Allergies: denies known drug allergies.  
• Social/obstetric: pregnancy unlikely per patient. No additional social data provided.

Objective:
(Tele-consultation; no vitals or direct examination possible)  
• Patient reports: no limb weakness, no gait disturbance, able to walk straight, no speech difficulty.  
• No clinical neuro-deficit observed via video.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Acute unilateral headache with visual aura  
   – Assessment / likely diagnosis: Migraine with aura (DDx #1, likelihood High).  
   – Differential diagnosis:  
     • Subarachnoid haemorrhage (DDx, Medium)—sudden onset, vomiting but pain only 6/10; no neck stiffness/LOC.  
     • Carotid or vertebral artery dissection (DDx, Low-Medium)—unilateral pain & visual disturbance; no neck pain/trauma.  
     • Acute meningitis/encephalitis (DDx, Low)—photophobia & vomiting but afebrile, no neck stiffness.  
     • Intracranial mass (DDx, Low)—new headache with visual change; sudden onset argues against.  
   – Investigations planned: none immediately; full neurological examination at same-day GP visit. Escalate to ED if red-flag symptoms emerge.  
   – Treatment planned: ibuprofen plus OTC anti-sickness agent; advise sugary carbonated drink. Escalate to specific migraine therapy if inadequate response.  
   – Relevant referrals: ED if red-flag features; consider neurology referral if recurrent or atypical.

2. Associated nausea/vomiting  
   – Assessment: part of migraine episode.  
   – Differential: as per Issue 1.  
   – Treatment: anti-sickness medication (dose/route/frequency not documented), oral hydration with sugary fluids.

3. Health anxiety about serious intracranial pathology  
   – Assessment: patient expresses fear of tumour/stroke.  
   – Plan: provided education on migraine features vs serious causes; arranged prompt review and clear safety-netting to reduce anxiety.

Quality checks:
● Missing elements: no vitals recorded; no formal neuro examination; medication doses/routes/frequencies not documented; no social history (smoking, alcohol) captured.  
● Transcript/DDx conflicts: none noted.  
● Transcript quality: clear audio; brief temporary connection drop but clinical content preserved.
